checkpoints: Understand when async matters in a Flask context
Install flask[async] and write an async view function
Make an async HTTP call with httpx inside a view
Compare response times between sync and async I/O-bound routes

content.value: Flask 2.0+ supports async view functions natively. Declare a view with async def and await I/O-bound calls — HTTP requests to external APIs, slow database queries — inside it. This prevents blocking the thread while waiting. Use httpx.AsyncClient() as an async HTTP client. The caveat: Flask still runs in a synchronous WSGI context by default; for full async throughput you need an ASGI server like Hypercorn or a migration to FastAPI. Async Flask is most useful when a single request fans out to multiple external services concurrently.

checkpoints: Run Redis locally with Docker
Install Flask-Caching and configure the Redis backend
Cache an expensive route response with @cache.cached()
Cache at the function level with @cache.memoize()
Manually invalidate a cache key after a data mutation

content.value: Caching eliminates redundant computation and database load. Redis is the standard in-memory cache for Python backends. Flask-Caching wraps Redis with a clean API: @cache.cached(timeout=60) caches the entire route response for 60 seconds. @cache.memoize() caches based on function arguments — useful for functions called with different parameters. Cache invalidation is the hard part: after a write operation, call cache.delete_memoized(my_function, arg) or use a cache key prefix per resource that you can bust with cache.delete_many(). Always measure cache hit rates in production.

checkpoints: Install Celery and configure it with a Redis broker
Define a task with the @celery.task decorator
Trigger the task from a Flask route with .delay()
Poll task status from the client using the task ID
Handle task retries and failure states

content.value: Long-running operations (sending emails, processing uploads, generating reports) should never block an HTTP request. Celery offloads them to a worker process. Define a task: @celery.task def send_email(user_id): ... . In your route, call send_email.delay(user_id) — this returns immediately with a task ID. The client can poll GET /tasks/<task_id> to check progress. Configure retries with @celery.task(max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=60). Redis serves as both the message broker (task queue) and result backend. In production, run workers with celery -A app.celery worker --loglevel=info.

checkpoints: Install Flask-Limiter and apply a global rate limit
Apply stricter limits to authentication endpoints
Add security headers with Flask-Talisman
Test rate limit behavior with a simple loop script

content.value: Public APIs need protection against abuse. Flask-Limiter applies rate limits declaratively: @limiter.limit('5 per minute') on the login route prevents brute-force attacks. Use Redis as the storage backend so limits are shared across multiple workers. Flask-Talisman adds HTTP security headers in one line: Talisman(app) enables HTTPS-only, sets X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, and Content-Security-Policy. Review the CSP carefully — a misconfigured CSP breaks legitimate resources. These two libraries cover the most common security baseline for production Flask APIs.

checkpoints: Write a Dockerfile for the Flask app
Build and run the container locally
Write a docker-compose.yml for Flask, PostgreSQL, and Redis
Use environment variables via docker-compose for secrets
Run database migrations inside the container on startup

content.value: Docker packages your app and its dependencies into a portable container. The Dockerfile starts from python:3.11-slim, installs requirements.txt, copies your source, and defines CMD ["gunicorn", "app:create_app()"]. docker-compose orchestrates multiple services: your Flask app, a PostgreSQL container, and a Redis container — each in its own service with a named network for inter-service communication. Pass secrets as environment variables in docker-compose.yml (and override with a .env file). Add a healthcheck to the Flask service so dependent services wait for it to be ready.

checkpoints: Design a URL versioning strategy: /api/v1/...
Register versioned blueprints in the factory
Generate OpenAPI documentation with flask-smorest
Expose a Swagger UI at /docs
Write a deprecation strategy for v1 when v2 launches

content.value: Production APIs change over time, but you can't break existing clients. URL versioning (/api/v1/, /api/v2/) is the simplest strategy — register each version as a separate blueprint. flask-smorest integrates marshmallow schemas with OpenAPI spec generation automatically. Annotate your routes with @blp.arguments(MySchema) and @blp.response(200, MySchema) and flask-smorest builds the spec. Expose Swagger UI at /api/docs for interactive exploration. Establish a deprecation policy: announce v2, support v1 for six months, then sunset it. Document the policy in your README.

checkpoints: Containerize the app with Docker and docker-compose
Add Redis caching to at least one expensive endpoint
Offload one operation to a Celery background task
Apply rate limiting to auth endpoints
Generate OpenAPI docs with Swagger UI
Write a deployment README with setup instructions

content.value: Your capstone is a deployment-ready API that demonstrates professional engineering practices. Take an existing Flask API (your notes app or a new domain) and harden it: containerize it, add caching, offload a background task, lock down auth endpoints with rate limiting, and generate API documentation. The deployment README should let a colleague spin up the entire stack with two commands. This level of completeness — security, performance, observability, documentation — is what distinguishes a production API from a prototype.
